title: Assessing the potential of interior methods for nonlinear optimization
contribution: Second (OCR) read of the 2003 benchmark of KNITRO 1.00 and LOQO 4.05 against SNOPT 5.3-4 and FilterSQP 1.0. It recovers the numbers: 509 of 740 CUTE/AMPL problems (December 2000), 30 CPU minutes and 1000 major iterations counted as failures, tolerance 1e-6 on all solvers, CPU times only above 100 variables. Table 1's solved counts put a different code first in each class (LOQO unconstrained 171/187; KNITRO equality 61/64 and general n>=100 58/67; SNOPT general 235/258), and the scale-up claim rests on 30 problems with more than 1000 variables and 6 with more than 10,000.
problem_entry: As in round 1 (c04): are the interior methods in LOQO and KNITRO competitive with established large-scale SQP codes, and where are they weak? Size range now readable: CUTE problems with up to 10,000 variables or constraints (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: Codes chosen along named axes and reduced to their algorithmic core per class (pp. 2, 7, 10, 12–13), as in c04. Now readable: LOQO's squared l2 penalty merit (4) and its per-iteration barrier rule (11), which lets mu increase, mu = 0.1*min(...)^3 * s'y/q with xi = min s_i y_i/(y's/q) (pp. 3–4, 12; page images); KNITRO's non-squared merit (6), mu cut by a fixed factor of five, initial mu always 0.1, and a per-iteration cost of one factorization of (5), ncg+2 backsolves and ncg Hessian-vector products (pp. 4, 12–13, 15); SNOPT's dense reduced-Hessian BFGS that switches to limited memory for large n (p. 5); FilterSQP's l-infinity trust region (pp. 6–7). KNITRO's global theory is ref. [4] = Byrd–Gilbert–Nocedal 2000 (S009) and its rate theory ref. [6] (pp. 5, 16).
assumptions: 509 problems: the subset of the 740 Benson–Vanderbei AMPL/CUTE problems (December 2000) left after excluding LP, QP, feasibility and bound-only problems, at default dimensions. Class sizes: 187 unconstrained (95 with n>=100), 64 equality (27), 258 general (67). Sun Ultra 5, 385Mb, SunOS 5.7, double precision, all defaults. Limits of 30 CPU minutes and 1000 major iterations count as failures; tolerance 1e-6 on all solvers (exponent read on the page image); KNITRO's stopping test modified to match SNOPT's, with final-precision differences 'not significant'. CPU times reported only for 'more than 100 variables' (p. 6), while p. 9 and Table 1 use n>=100. SNOPT first-order only; runs made in fall 2000 (pp. 6–7, 15).
proof_devices: Dolan–Moré log2 performance profile defined as (8)–(9): r_ps = t_ps/t*_p, a large M for failures, pi_s(tau) = share of problems with log2 r <= tau, plotted for tau in [0, 12]; cited from the 2001 Argonne report ANL/MCS-P861-1200 (pp. 8, 16).
Size-artefact test: 16 CUTE problems, each in three versions with dimensions generally in the thousands, KNITRO against SNOPT; no clear trend (p. 14).
Iteration comparison: KNITRO needs fewer iterations than LOQO on about 2/3 of the problems with n>=50; iterations are not tabulated (p. 14).

Accounting corrections: LOQO's extra evaluation per iteration discounted; LOQO's unconstrained stopping test often less demanding; SNOPT may undercount evaluations when the objective is linear (pp. 10, 14).
experiments: Table 1 (p. 15; the two n>=100 rows of the unconstrained and equality classes read on the page image), problems solved as filterSQP/LOQO/KNITRO/SNOPT/sample: unconstrained all 120/171/145/120/187, n>=100 33/83/67/35/95; equality all 51/57/61/48/64, n>=100 13/20/24/12/27; general all 226/218/234/235/258, n>=100 47/39/58/50/67. My sums: over all 509, LOQO 446, KNITRO 440, SNOPT 403, filterSQP 397; over the 189 problems with n>=100, KNITRO 149, LOQO 142, SNOPT 97, filterSQP 93. CPU profiles cover 95/27/67 problems and evaluation profiles 187/64/258 (Figs. 1–6, pp. 8–14). Large problems: 30 with more than 1000 variables and 6 with more than 10,000; per-code counts for them are not printed (p. 15). KNITRO's own weaknesses: the fixed initial mu = 0.1 'can be highly detrimental in some cases', and its time per iteration exceeds LOQO's on 'a significant percentage' of the problems (p. 15).
positioning: As in c04: refuses to rank (p. 2) and thanks the rival developers (p. 16). Legible references: KNITRO [5] = Byrd–Hribar–Nocedal (S008); KNITRO's theory [4] = S009; SNOPT's limited-memory evaluation [19] = the first author's own 2001 L-BFGS study (pp. 16–17). Recommends that SNOPT replace its dense quasi-Newton matrix by a limited-memory one (pp. 9–10).
writing: As in c04. The ranking warning and the 'what this study can and cannot achieve' paragraph open the paper (§1, p. 2), before any result. Caution flags beside the results are attached to particular observations (pp. 10, 11, 14). The robustness table appears only in the final remarks (p. 15).
limits_future: The scale-up claim is hedged ('Based on this small sample') and rests on 36 large problems with no per-code counts (p. 15). Table 1's general n>=100 cut puts KNITRO highest (58/67) and LOQO lowest (39/67), uncommented in the text (my reading). To-do items for KNITRO: a preconditioner and an adaptive initial barrier parameter (pp. 15–16).

method_links.note: Every protocol number now readable: aligned stopping test, limits counted as failures, one tolerance 1e-6, CPU size threshold, accounting corrections, full solved-count table with the own code's losses (145 vs LOQO's 171 of 187 unconstrained). Resolves the SKILL.md Method 1 warning that the 2003 digits are unreadable; steps 4, 5 and 7 can cite S078 pp. 6–7.
No code wins every class: LOQO leads unconstrained, KNITRO equality and general n>=100, and the first-order SNOPT general 'all' by one problem (235 vs 234).

Hard-coded barrier choices recorded with their values (fixed factor-of-five decrease, initial mu = 0.1); the latter becomes a named to-do item (adaptive initial mu). Its link to KNITRO's later barrier options is inferred from timing only.

Context only: the overview names what blocks theory for the rival LOQO (a dynamic barrier rule, a non-exact penalty merit) and cites S009 as the theory of a KNITRO-like algorithm; S061 analyses KNITRO's fixed-mu regime (S061 p. 17).

transferable: Build a size-stratified robustness table: solved counts per class for all problems and for n>=100, with the sample size in its own column (p. 15).
Put the protocol's numbers in one place: test-set provenance with date and count, machine, failure limits, a single tolerance (pp. 6–7).
Date the runs in a footnote and say which rival version did not exist then (p. 7).
Test a tempting explanation with a scaled family (16 problems x 3 sizes) and print the null result (p. 14).
Attach the sample size to any scaling claim (30 problems over 1000 variables, 6 over 10,000) and hedge accordingly (p. 15).
coauthors: José Luis Morales, Richard A. Waltz, Guanghui Liu, Jean-Pierre Goux

quotes.text: A limit of 30 minutes of CPU time, and 1000 major iterations, were imposed for each problem; if one of these limits was reached the code was considered to have failed.
Our set of inequality constrained problems contained 30 problems with more than 1000 variables, and only 6 problems with more than 10,000 variables.

title: On the convergence of Newton iterations to non-stationary points
contribution: Second (OCR) read of Report OTC 2001/01 (April 23, 2001), published in Math. Program. 2004. It recovers the theorem statements and data: Theorem 2.2's sign dichotomy on D2phi(z;v_n) under rank F'(z) = n-1 and F(z) not in R(F'(z)); Lemma 3.2 for minimization; Theorem 4.1 for a feasible primal-dual method with barrier merit. Three tables: regularized Newton hits 1000 iterations for every rho>0 on Powell's example (best final ||F|| 1.6e-4 against tolerance 1e-6), LMDER solves it in 12 iterations, and a KKT-norm primal-dual run stalls with ||grad phi_mu|| at about 0.878.
problem_entry: As in c04. Now readable: Powell's example F(x,y) = (x, 10x/(x+0.1)+2y^2), started at (3,1) with an exact line search, converges to z = (1.8016, 0) on the singular x-axis (pp. 3–4, page images). Fletcher's question is quoted from Practical Methods of Optimization, 2nd ed., p. 121 (p. 14). The report follows the Wächter–Biegler example (Math. Program. 88(3), 2000) within a year (pp. 1, 25).
key_idea: Theorem 2.2 (p. 5): alpha_k is the first local minimizer of phi = 0.5||F||^2, rank F'(z) = n-1 (2.6a) and F(z) not in R(F'(z)) (2.6b). If D2phi(z;v_n) = sum F_i(z) v_n' Hess F_i(z) v_n > 0, the displacements become arbitrarily small near z; if it is < 0, they stay bounded below by T. Extended to the first Wolfe interval with 0<eta<beta<1 (p. 8) and, in Theorem 2.3, to any rank deficiency via definiteness of sum F_i Hess F_i on the null space (p. 10). (2.6b) is shown necessary by F = (x^2+y^2, y^2) at (2,0) and by Example 2, F = (x+y^2, 2(x-1)y) on the line {(1,y)}, where ||grad phi|| >= 1 (pp. 10–11). Lemma 3.2 (p. 14): positive definite Hessians, Wolfe steps, rank n-1 and grad f(z) not in R(Hess f(z)) imply that the iterates stay away from z. Algorithm 1 (p. 20): B_k = Hess L + A G^-1 Lambda A' or a modification; B_k d = -grad psi_mu; Wolfe steps on psi_mu; lambda step largest in [0,1] with lambda_{k+1} >= (1-tau) lambda_k, tau = 0.995. Theorem 4.1: under A1–A3 every limit point is stationary for the barrier function. Safeguard (p. 22): multipliers capped at c*mu/g_i, c>1, plus modified Cholesky; inactive near a regular solution.
assumptions: F in C^2; (2.6a)/(2.6b); first local minimizer or first Wolfe interval, backtracking excluded (pp. 3, 5, 8). Minimization: Hess f(x_k) positive definite, rank n-1 (p. 14). Constrained case: mu fixed until the barrier problem is solved (p. 17); strictly feasible iterates; A1 f bounded below on the feasible region; A2 Hess f, Hess g_i and grad g_i bounded on its convex hull; A3 eigenvalues of B_k bounded above and away from zero (p. 20).
proof_devices: ||d_k|| -> infinity and d_k/||d_k|| -> v_n; restriction h_k(tau) = phi(x_k + tau d_k/||d_k||) with h_k'(0) = -||F||^2/||d_k|| < 0 (p. 6).

Case (i): h_k'' >= rho/2 for tau <= T and |h_k'(0)| < rho T/4, so the Taylor bound puts the first local minimizer at tau_k < -4 h_k'(0)/rho -> 0. Case (ii): h_k'' <= rho/2 < 0, so all minimizers lie in [T, infinity) (pp. 7–8; page image).

Lemma 3.2 by contradiction along a subsequence converging to z: the first Wolfe condition forces tau_k -> 0, while the curvature condition and the mean-value theorem keep tau_k bounded below because h_k'(0) stays bounded away from zero (pp. 15–16).

Theorem 4.1, Zoutendijk-type: iterates in S_sigma = {g >= sigma e}; grad psi_mu is Lipschitz (L) on S_sigma/2. Case (a): decrease >= eta(1-beta)/L (grad psi'd/||d||)^2. Case (b): step >= sigma/(2C), so decrease >= -(eta sigma/2C) grad psi'd/||d||. Hence -grad psi'd/||d|| -> 0, and the eigenvalue bounds give that this quantity is >= (beta2/beta1)||grad psi_mu|| (pp. 21–22; page images).
Necessity of a hypothesis via two 2-variable systems, one where the conclusion fails and one where it holds (pp. 10–11); affine change of variables maps Example 4 onto Example 2 (p. 23).
Theorem prediction plotted: -h'(0)/h''(0) over the grid [1,3]x[-1,1] (p. 9); hypotheses (2.6), (2.8) checked at the numerical limit point of Example 3 (p. 18).
experiments: Table 1 (p. 12): regularized Newton (2.31), used when the eigenvalues of F'F fall below rho, on Powell's example from (1.7, 0.1), backtracking, stop at ||F||<1e-6 or after 100 line-search trials, limit 1000 iterations. Results as rho / iterations / regularized steps / final ||F|| / final ||grad phi||: 0 / 25 (line search failed) / 0 / 9.585 / 4.662; sqrt(macheps) / 1000 / 495 / 9.585 / 4.662; 1e-4 / 1000 / 452 / 9.563 / 4.774; 1e-2 / 1000 / 940 / 1.629e-4 / 9.034e-7; 1e-1 / 1000 / 994 / 1.392e-3 / 1.492e-5. The largest eigenvalue of F'F is of order 100. SVD regularization with rho = 0.1 is still O(1e-2) from the solution after 1000 iterations, 963 of them modified (p. 12). Table 2 (p. 13): LMDER solves the problem in 12 iterations (final ||F|| 2.788e-7), rejecting steps 1 and 6, with rho in [0, 401] and rho = 0 in the last 4 iterations; the text gives rho = 4.010e-02 where the table prints 4.010e+02. Table 3 (p. 18): Example 3, min (1/3)(x-1)^3 + x s.t. x >= 0, mu = 0.01, from (5,1), solution about (5e-3, 1.99). Alpha_k falls from 1 to 3.47e-18 and cos(grad phi_mu, d_k) from -0.979 to -6.93e-10; phi_mu stays at 0.435 and ||grad phi_mu|| at about 0.878; the iterates stall at (0.96364, 0.070085), and the line search fails at iteration 15.
positioning: As in c04. Answers Wächter–Biegler (2000) within a year and credits Powell, Wächter–Biegler and Fletcher by name (pp. 1–2, 14, 22, 25). Restates the Wächter–Biegler instance, x1^2 - x2 - 1 = 0, x1 - x3 - 2 = 0, x2, x3 >= 0 (p. 23).
writing: As in c04. The theorem is turned into an implementation signature: a step-size test fires, or the line search fails because phi(x_k + alpha_k d_k) = phi(x_k) in finite precision (p. 8). Report-version slips: references to a nonexistent 'step 4' (p. 20), 'Step 2' for the Hessian modification made in Step 1 (p. 22), the rho mismatch in Table 2 (p. 13), and a truncated exponent in the final iterate (p. 18). The journal version was not checked.
limits_future: As in c04. Example 4 defeats 'any line search algorithm whose search direction d satisfies the linearization of the constraints', and no remedy is given (pp. 23–24). That methods relaxing the linearized constraints (e.g. a trust-region normal step) fall outside the hypothesis is my inference, not the paper's claim.

method_links.note: Theory separates practical variants, now with numbers: the KKT-norm merit stalls with ||grad phi_mu|| = 0.878, while the barrier merit is safe by Theorem 4.1; a line search on ||F|| behaves differently from one on f; regularization fails at 1000 iterations while a trust region needs 12. The prediction is plotted on a grid and the hypotheses are checked at the numerical limit point (counterpart to step 4).
The Wächter–Biegler counterexample is treated as a specification, credited by name and answered within a year (report dated April 23, 2001).

The answer is an analysis, a provably safe algorithm class (Algorithm 1) and a new failure example, not a production variant; the infeasible case is left without a fix. Step 4's 'build the variant' and Workflow E step 2 hold only as a paper algorithm.

The comforting assumption that regularization fixes the difficulty is tested on a five-value rho grid plus an SVD variant and refuted (all rho>0 hit 1000 iterations; best final ||F|| 1.6e-4 against tolerance 1e-6).
Names the failing component (the merit function), keeps the Newton engine and changes only the merit function plus a Hessian safeguard. No estimate-driven repair and no recovery path.

transferable: Print the per-iteration diagnostics that expose the mechanism: step length, cosine between direction and merit gradient, merit value and its gradient norm (p. 18).

Run the common fix over a grid of its parameter (rho = 0, sqrt(macheps), 1e-4, 1e-2, 1e-1), report iterations, activations and final residuals, then run an off-the-shelf alternative from the same start (pp. 12–13).
State the result as a sign dichotomy along the null direction and plot the predicted quantity -h'(0)/h''(0) on a grid (pp. 5, 9).
Show that a hypothesis is necessary with two small systems: one where the conclusion fails without it and one where it holds anyway (pp. 10–11).
Use Hessian safeguards that provably switch off near a regular solution: multipliers capped at c*mu/g_i with c>1, and modified Cholesky (p. 22).

Triage signature: if alpha_k -> 0 and cos(grad phi, d_k) -> 0 while ||grad phi|| stays bounded away from zero, suspect a singular non-stationary point and check the merit function before the direction (pp. 8, 18).

quotes.text: It is clear that the conditions of Theorem 2.2 can lead to convergence to a singular non-stationary point in some cases, but whether it always does is an open question.
The Levenberg-Morrison-Marquardt method was very efficient … in this example, taking only 12 iterations to solve the problem to the prescribed accuracy.
